blocks.text: [III, 43] Both the Arabs and the Talmudists have taught us that the Hebrew קאת kaath is the same as קוק huk and kuk, a water bird with a long neck. But since this is not enough, because there are many water birds with long necks, the Greeks and Jerome point us to the pelican; and I gladly embrace this rendering as the truest. For the origin of the word leads us to it, which plainly derives from the verb קאה kaah, that is, to vomit. Hence Baal Hatturim: הקאת דרכו להקיא מאכלו, "the kaath is accustomed to vomit up its food." And lest the final Tav be thought an obstacle, Rabbi Jonah teaches that it is a formative of the noun, and that the true root is קאה kaah. And Kimchi cites a poet who says קאות kaoth in the plural. So, just as from פרה comes פרת for the Euphrates, and שחת, pit, from שחה, so קאת, pelican, comes from קאה ^{(4)}. And why it is named from vomiting is not obscure to those who know that the pelican brings back up shells it has already swallowed, after they have been opened by the heat of its belly, so as to pick out the edible parts from them. The ancient writers assert this with such agreement that the matter cannot be called into doubt. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 10: Οἱ δὲ πελεκᾶνες, οἱ ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γινόμενοι, καταπίνουσι τὰς μεγάλας κόγχας καὶ λείας· ὅταν δὲ ἐν τῷ πρὸ τῆς κοιλίας τόπῳ πέψωσιν, ἐξεμοῦσιν, ἵνα χασκουσῶν τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντες ἐσθίωσι. [Hoi de pelekanes, hoi en tois potamois ginomenoi, katapinousi tas megalas konchas kai leias; hotan de en tō pro tēs koilias topō pepsōsin, exemousin, hina chaskousōn ta krea exaphountes esthiōsi.] "River pelicans swallow large smooth shells, and when these have been cooked in the stomach they vomit them up, so as to take the flesh out of them as they gape and eat it." And in the book of Marvels [ch. 13]: Φασὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας τὰς ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γενομένας κόγχας ὀρύττοντας κατεσθίειν· ἔπειτα, ὅταν πλῆθος εἰσφορήσωσιν αὐτῶν, ἐξεμεῖν, εἶθ᾽ οὕτως τὰ μὲν κρέα ἐσθίειν τῶν κογχῶν, τῶν δὲ ὀστράκων μὴ ἅπτεσθαι. [Phasi tous pelekanas tas en tois potamois genomenas konchas oryttontas katesthiein; epeita, hotan plēthos eisphorēsōsin autōn, exemein, eith' houtōs ta men krea esthiein tōn konchōn, tōn de ostrakōn mē haptesthai.] "They say that pelicans devour shells dug out of the rivers, and, having taken in a quantity of them, soon vomit them up, so that they pick out the flesh to eat and leave the shells alone." Antigonus of Carystus, Story 47: Τοὺς δὲ πελεκᾶνας τὰς θηλείας κόγχας καταπίνειν ἱστορεῖ· ἔπειτα ὀλίγας κατασχόντας ἐν τῷ ἄνω τῆς κοιλίας ἐξεμεῖν κεχηνυίας· εἶτα οὕτω τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντας ἐσθίειν. [Tous de pelekanas tas thēleias konchas katapinein historei; epeita oligas kataschontas en tō anō tēs koilias exemein kechēnuias; eita houtō ta krea exaphountas esthiein.] This suffers from three errors: for τὰς θηλείας κόγχας [tas thēleias konchas], female shells, read τὰς λείας κόγχας [tas leias konchas], smooth shells, as in Aristotle; for ἱστορεῖ [historei], he relates, read ἱστορεῖται [historeitai], it is related; and for ὀλίγας κατασχόντας [oligas kataschontas], having retained small ones, read ὀλίγον κατασχόντας [oligon kataschontas], having retained them a little while. It should therefore be translated thus: "It is related that pelicans swallow smooth shells; then, [III, 44] after retaining them a little while in the top of the stomach, they vomit them up gaping, and so take out the flesh and eat it." Pliny, book 10, chapter 40: "The same bird, when it has filled itself with swallowed shells, vomits them up cooked by the heat of its belly, and so picks out the edible parts from them, rejecting the shells." Aelian, History of Animals, book 3, chapter 20: Οἱ πελεκᾶνες, ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς κόγχας περιχαίνοντες· εἶτα καταπίνουσιν· ἔνδον δὲ καὶ ἐν μυχῷ τῆς γαστρὸς ὑποθάλψαντες ἀνεμοῦσιν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀστράκια ἐκ τῆς ἀλέας διέστη ὡσπεροῦν τῶν ἑφθῶν. οἱ δὲ ἐξορύττουσι τὰ κρέα, καὶ ἔχουσι δεῖπνον. [Hoi pelekanes, en tois potamois konchas perichainontes; eita katapinousin; endon de kai en mychō tēs gastros hypothalpsantes anemousin, kai ta men ostrakia ek tēs aleas diestē hōsperoun tōn hephthōn. hoi de exoryttousi ta krea, kai echousi deipnon.] "Spoonbills gape after river shells and swallow them; and having warmed them in the depth of the stomach they vomit them up. And from the shells, forced apart by the heat of the belly, as if they had been cooked, they dig out the flesh for food." Almost the same is found in Apostolius, Century 15, Proverb 93. Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, after saying that the shells they swallow are loosened by the heat of the throat, says: ἐξεμέσαντες οὖν αὐτὰς εὐμαρῶς τὸ ἐδώδιμον αὐτῶν [exemesantes oun autas eumarōs to edōdimon autōn] [col. 295] κατεσθίουσιν [katesthiousin], "having vomited them up, they easily eat what is edible." Philes, On Animals, chapter 8:

Κόγχην δὲ πελεκὰν ἐμβαλὼν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις, Κἀνάπαλιν αὐτὴν ἐξενεγκὼν ὀστράκοις Τὸ σαρκίον βέβρωκε ληφθὲν εὐστόχως. [Konchēn de pelekan embalōn tois enkatois, Kanapalin autēn exenenkōn ostrakois To sarkion bebrōke lēphthen eustochōs.]

"The pelican, having sent a shell down into its innards and brought it back up again, skilfully feeds on the flesh taken out of the shell." Pisides too, On the Creation of the World, says that they send the shells down into the fire of their innards, since they cannot be opened otherwise:

Λύσιν δὲ πάσχει τῶν πτυχῶν ἡ στεῤῥότης, Τῇ θερμότητι τῶν ἔσω χαυνουμένη. Θᾶττον δὲ τὰς πρὶν ἐξεμοῦντες συνδέσεις, Γυμνῇ διαρπάζουσι τὰς σάρκας μάχῃ, Τὴν ὀστρακώδη μὴ φορούσας ἀσπίδα. [Lysin de paschei tōn ptychōn hē sterrotēs, Tē thermotēti tōn esō chaunoumenē. Thatton de tas prin exemountes syndeseis, Gymnē diarpazousi tas sarkas machē, Tēn ostrakōdē mē phorousas aspida.]
